analysis.one_liner: Requires employers to pay equal wages for jobs of equivalent skill, effort, and responsibility, regardless of sex, race, or national origin.
analysis.headline: The Fair Pay Act of 1997, with 64 cosponsors, never received a committee vote or a floor vote; it died in the House Education and the Workforce Committee when the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Fair Labor Standards Act to bar paying workers less because of their sex, race, or national origin — not just for the exact same job, but for different jobs whose overall demands (skill, effort, responsibility, working conditions) are equivalent. It would have protected employees who discuss or compare wages, let wage-discrimination cases proceed as class actions, and required employers to report pay data by race and sex to the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission. It was referred to a House committee and its subcommittees and never went any further.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers — disproportionately women and people of color — in jobs that pay less than equivalent jobs held by men or white workers. The bill's findings cite studies finding large unexplained wage gaps between white and non-white workers and a pattern of female-dominated jobs paying below average for equivalent work. Workers who compared or discussed wages would gain explicit protection from retaliation, and prevailing plaintiffs could recover expert-witness fees and sue as a class.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Women and workers of color in underpaid jobs

how_it_helps.text: Bars paying lower wages for jobs whose combined skill, effort, responsibility, and working conditions are equivalent, not just for identical work — the existing law only covered 'equal work'. [S2] [S3]
Protects employees from being fired, coerced, or intimidated for asking about, disclosing, or comparing wages, or for helping an investigation under the law. [S2] [S3]
Lets wage-discrimination cases proceed as class actions and awards expert-witness fees to prevailing plaintiffs, making lawsuits practical for low-paid workers. [S2] [S3]

Requires employers to file annual public reports to the EEOC showing pay rates by job classification together with the sex, race, and national origin of employees at each pay level, making pay gaps visible. [S2] [S3]
Preserves existing seniority, merit, and production-based pay systems as lawful exceptions, so pay differences tied to performance or tenure remain allowed. [S2] [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Employers whose current pay structures would fail the equivalent-jobs test would bear the cost of raising wages to comply — the bill explicitly forbids compliance by cutting anyone's pay. All covered employers would also face new recordkeeping duties and an annual public wage report to the EEOC. Some of the wage costs could ultimately show up in prices or hiring decisions.

drawbacks.text: 'Equivalent jobs' is a hard standard to apply: the bill requires comparing dissimilar jobs (say, a nurse and a warehouse worker) on a composite of skill, effort, responsibility, and working conditions, which invites extensive litigation and gives courts and the EEOC wide discretion to re-rate jobs. [S3]

Covered employers would face ongoing compliance costs: preserving wage-setting records, filing annual signed reports, and disclosing pay by race and sex publicly, which critics would call a significant paperwork and competitive burden, particularly for smaller firms. [S3]
Because the bill bars employers from lowering wages to comply, the entire cost of adjustment falls on employers, who might respond in ways the bill cannot control, such as slower hiring. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real, documented gap — pay differences between equivalent jobs along sex, race, and national-origin lines that existing 'equal pay for equal work' law does not reach — and its class-action, fee, and wage-transparency provisions would have given low-paid workers realistic tools to use it. The honest cost is that comparing dissimilar jobs is inherently judgment-laden, so employers would have faced genuine uncertainty and litigation risk, and the annual public pay reports would be a significant compliance burden. On balance it is a substantial pro-worker measure with real administrative and litigation costs that its sponsors accepted as the price of enforcement.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, which sent it to two subcommittees; no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Eleanor Holmes Norton introduced the bill on April 10, 1997, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce. [S5]
On April 28, 1997, it was referred to two subcommittees — Employer-Employee Relations and Workforce Protections — and no further action was ever recorded. [S5]
The bill attracted 64 cosponsors, 62 Democrats, 1 Republican, and 1 independent, but never reached a committee vote or the House floor. [S1] [S4] [S5]
The 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, with the bill still stalled in committee. [S1]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers whose pay structures would have failed an equivalent-jobs test are better off: no wage adjustments, no annual public pay reports, and no expanded class-action exposure. Nothing changed for the workers the bill was written for.

sides.party_line_note: 62 of the bill's 64 cosponsors were Democrats, with one Republican and one independent; the House majority that never acted on it was Republican. [S4] [S5]

industries.industry: Covered employers, especially in female- and minority-dominated low-wage sectors (retail, care work, services)
industries.note: The bill would have forced employers to raise wages wherever jobs of equivalent demands were paid unequally along sex, race, or national-origin lines, and barred them from cutting anyone's pay to comply. Its defeat left existing pay structures untouched. [S3]

All covered employers would have had to preserve wage-setting records and file an annual public report to the EEOC disclosing pay rates by job classification and employee sex, race, and national origin. Compliance costs, though modest relative to wage adjustment, were real. [S3]
The bill would have barred unions from causing employers to discriminate in wages and given members a stronger legal floor, complementing collective bargaining over pay. [S3]
The bill would have given the EEOC new enforcement data, reporting rules, research, and technical-assistance duties, expanding the agency's role in policing pay. [S2] [S3]
